n: Two of Pharaoh’s personal servants fell out of favor: his cupbearer and his chief baker, both trusted with the king’s food and drink.

f.g: cupbearer—served the king’s wine and guarded against poison

n: Pharaoh grew angry with these two chief officials. Their offense isn’t specified.
Both were placed in custody in the same prison as Joseph. God was placing the right people in Joseph’s path.
Joseph was assigned to serve these high-ranking prisoners, and they remained there for some time.
On the same night, each man had a dream with its own special meaning.

f.w: according to the interpretation of his dream
f.g: each dream had its own significance

n: Joseph noticed their sad faces. Even in prison he paid attention to the feelings of others.
Joseph kindly asks why they look so troubled today.
They had no dream interpreter—Egypt’s professional interpreters were out of reach. Joseph points them to God as the true source of understanding.

f.w: Do not interpretations belong to God?

n: The cupbearer goes first, describing a grapevine that appeared before him.
The vine had three branches that budded, blossomed, and ripened all at once—a picture of quick change.
In the dream he pressed the grapes into Pharaoh’s cup and handed it to him—his usual job, a hopeful sign.
Joseph explains: the three branches mean three days.
In three days Pharaoh would “lift up his head”—restore him to honor—and he would serve Pharaoh’s cup again.

f.g: an idiom for restoring someone to favor

n: Joseph asks a simple favor: remember me to Pharaoh. Joseph trusted God but also took reasonable action to seek his own freedom.
Joseph briefly explains his innocence: he was kidnapped from his homeland and had done nothing to deserve prison.

f.g: literally “the pit,” the same word used for the cistern in Genesis 37:24

n: Encouraged by the good news, the baker tells his dream too, about three baskets on his head.

f.g: possibly baskets of white bread, or wicker baskets

n: Birds ate Pharaoh’s baked goods from the top basket—an ominous sign, since the baker could not protect the king’s food.
Joseph interprets this dream also as three days.
Joseph honestly delivers terrible news: Pharaoh would lift the baker’s head “off”—a grim wordplay meaning execution. A true servant of God tells the truth even when it hurts.

f.w: lift up thy head from off thee
f.g: wordplay on verse 13 — here meaning beheading
display the body on a pole, a public disgrace

n: On the third day, Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast and called for both men, deciding their fates before his court.
The cupbearer was restored to his position, just as Joseph said.
The baker was executed, exactly as Joseph had interpreted. God’s word through Joseph proved true in both cases.
But the cupbearer forgot Joseph. Joseph would wait two more years in prison—a reminder that God’s timing often requires patience.
